items.stem: An app runs as six identical copies behind a load balancer. Each copy can do everything the app does. How should you describe it?

options.text: A monolith, scaled out to six copies.
options.feedback: Every copy contains the whole application. Adding copies scales the application but does not split it.

options.text: Microservices, because there are six running programs.
options.feedback: Microservices are different applications, each doing one job. Six copies of the same program are still one application.

options.text: A distributed monolith, because it runs on several machines.
options.feedback: A distributed monolith is a set of services that depend on each other on every request. These copies do not call each other.

options.text: Neither, because a load balancer changes the design.
options.feedback: A load balancer only shares traffic between copies. The design is still a monolith.

items.stem: Before you try it: the application is quiet at 40 rps and busy at 400 rps. Which design uses less memory at each load?

options.text: The monolith at 40 rps, and the separate services at 400 rps.
options.feedback: At low load each service still needs at least one machine, so four services cost more. At higher load, sizing each part for its own need saves memory.

options.text: The separate services at both loads.
options.feedback: At 40 rps the four services need at least four machines, which uses more memory than the monolith.
At 400 rps most monolith workers are sized for the 400 MB PDF job even though few of them ever do it.

options.text: The separate services at 40 rps, and the monolith at 400 rps.
options.feedback: This reverses the pattern. Splitting pays off as load grows.

items.try: Drag Total load to 40 rps and read the two memory totals, then drag it to 400 rps and read them again.

items.stem: After a split, showing one enrollment page needs 4 calls to other services. Each service is up 99.9% of the time. About how often will that page fail because a service is down?

options.feedback: All four services must be up. 99.9% multiplied four times is about 99.6%, so about 0.4% of requests fail.
This is the failure rate of one service. The page needs four services, and any one of them can fail.
This overstates the effect. Each service fails about 0.1% of the time, so four of them fail about 0.4% of the time.

options.text: Almost never, because each service is very reliable.
options.feedback: Small failure rates add up when a request depends on several services at once.

items.try: Set Calls to other services to 4 and read Combined uptime.

items.stem: Which situation is the best reason to split one part of your application into its own service?

options.text: One part, such as PDF generation, needs far more memory and time than the rest.
options.feedback: A split pays off when one part's needs really differ from the rest. The memory comparison shows the saving.

options.text: Microservices are the modern way to build applications and look good on a CV.
options.feedback: Fashion is not a reason. Most failures start with a team that split before it had a reason.

options.text: Two parts need each other's data on every request, so splitting them looks tidy.
options.feedback: Parts that need each other on every request should stay together. Splitting them gives you a distributed monolith.

options.text: The team wants to practice running several services in the capstone project.
options.feedback: Splitting adds network calls, version drift, retry rules and scattered logs. A capstone rarely has a scaling problem that justifies this.
